title: Collections and Recovery: How an Auto Loan Becomes Delinquent and How It Is Charged Off
content:
The days past due on a loan of the Auto Loans line count calendar days since the earliest unsatisfied installment due date, and return to zero when every past-due installment is satisfied.

**Becoming delinquent.** The loan becomes delinquent when the days past due reach the number the product publishes for that point.

**Returning to active.** A delinquent loan returns to active when the days past due return to zero.

**Charge-off.** The remaining principal is charged off when the days past due reach the number the product publishes for that point. The charge-off writes off the whole of the unpaid principal, and the debt passes to recovery.

Both thresholds are read from the day count the bank's record of the loan carries, taken before either step, and correlated to the loan itself.

## Outside this policy

Repossession, settlements, hardship modifications and payment plans on delinquent loans are not matters this policy decides.

## How the day count is anchored

The day count is anchored on the earliest unsatisfied installment, not on the most recent one. A borrower who has missed three installments has a day count running from the oldest of them, which is why a single further payment may leave the count where it is unless it satisfies that oldest installment.

The count returns to zero only when every past-due installment is satisfied, not when the borrower has paid something toward them.
